column3: For the most part, this code is easy to reproduce: run.sh has commands to run both the models.py file and the clean.py file. The environment.yaml lists dependencies. I was able to find the code for plotting under models.py under the __main__ function. This plotting code makes more sense to have in either a jupyter notebook / separate function (instead of __main__), but the code is there and reproducible.
column4: Clean.py is easy to use and understand. The functions inside clean.py are all well-named and well-documented with their own docstrings. The user can get a clean dataframe with one line of code and the logic in the main block is easy to follow.
column5: The narrative is generally clear, well-structured, and reads well. I did not find any notable grammar mistakes. The report follows a clear outline. The findings sections had clear, specific claims that were easy to follow, and helpful visualizations were also provided.
column6: The data cleaning was described with reasonable details. This section correctly identifies the missing value codes. The GCS mismatch is described clearly, as is the age discrepancy. There are a few data inconsistencies that were not addressed: for example, when has_vomiting is 1 but the related fields to had_vomiting are inconsistent.
column7: The non-finding figures are relevant and help motivate the cleaning steps. There are 5 such figures. Figure 1’s four-panel overview (missingness, age distribution, GCS distribution, and outcome distribution) clearly supports the cleaning steps. Figure 2 backs up the discussion of the GCS mismatch and correlation patterns. Figures 3 and 4 align with the age-stratification and selection bias sections, respectively, and Figure 5 supports the GCS 14 vs. 15 comparison. None of the figures felt unhelpful / unneeded.
column11:
The left panel has hematoma location x vomiting/LOC and their corresponding PosCT rate. The right panel introduces a gender angle. I like the color choices and the ordering in the left panel. Just like the other figure, I think this one would benefit from increasing in size to make the annotations clearer. Also, there is no legend for the colors on the left panel. 

Overall, I really liked this figure. I thought it was very creative and informative. It was very interesting to see that vomiting had no effect on the frontal locations but serious effects on others locations.
column12: Yes, I found the reality check to be convincing. It cited the published Kuppermann et al. sensitivity figures and noted that the ciTBI rate and PosCT rate fall within expected ranges. "Typical pediatric ED population" is a little vague but the check was honest about its limitations.
column13: The stability check is relevant and well-executed. Excluding children under 2 is a meaningful perturbation as this population is a fairly large percentage of the dataset. All three findings persist after perturbation, and the specific numbers before/after are reported. One limitation of this section is that one of the findings isn't visually recreated with the perturbed data. . Still, this is a solid stability check.
